The line stops. The alarm says pick-up error. Within ten minutes three people are standing at the head: one swaps the nozzle, one re-teaches the part in the vision library, one opens the program. Forty minutes later the error comes back on the same slot, and nobody has looked at the feeder.

That is the expensive part of a feeder fault: it never announces itself as a feeder fault. A feeder that indexes a little short, or a lever that has worn, moves the component a few tenths of a millimetre away from the point the nozzle reaches for. The machine reports what it sees at the head, so every symptom points at the head. The real cause sits in the slot, quietly passing the blame along.

Use a three-question rule before anyone touches the nozzle or the program. One: does the error follow the slot or follow the feeder? Swap the feeder to another slot and watch. Two: if it follows the feeder, take the feeder off the line instead of adjusting it there. Three: check it against a fixed reference, not against the last technician's opinion. If the feeder is right on the reference, then go after the nozzle and the vision data.

The FUJI NXT Feeder Calibration Jig from Southern Machinery is that fixed reference. A 50X CCD camera with LED lighting looks at the pick-up window, the monitor shows a cross cursor set once against a standard calibration ruler, and a motor strikes the feeder lever in single or continuous steps so you can watch the part arrive. If the component centre and the cross cursor do not coincide, you adjust the feeder bolt-pin until they do, check the wheel gear and lock the screws.

Make it a standing habit: every feeder that is pulled for a pick-up error goes to the jig before it goes anywhere else, and the result goes into a one-line record - feeder ID, date, what was seen, what was adjusted. After a month the record tells you which feeders keep coming back, and those are the ones to repair or retire rather than re-adjust again.

A pallet of used NXT feeders at a good price looks like a win on the purchase order. It stops looking like one the first week they meet a running line.

A second-hand feeder carries a history you cannot see: hours of use, a dropped feeder, a lever that was bent and straightened, a repair done by someone in a hurry. None of that shows on the housing. What shows, eventually, is a slot that throws parts, and by then the feeder is mixed in with your good ones and the seller is no longer answering.

Treat incoming feeders the way you treat incoming components: nothing enters stock without an inspection record. Separate the batch, give each feeder an ID, check each one against the same reference, sort into three bins - accepted, adjust and recheck, reject - and only then put them on the feeder cart. The cost of the check is minutes per feeder; the cost of skipping it lands on the line.

The repair ticket says fixed. The feeder goes straight back into slot 23. Two hours later slot 23 is throwing parts again, and the night shift loses another hour proving that fixed did not mean right.

Repair restores a feeder mechanically; it does not prove the feeder feeds to the right position. A replaced spring, a new lever or a reassembled gear train can all shift the pick-up point slightly. Without a recheck, the first real test of the repair is production, which is the most expensive place to run a test.

Build one gate between the repair bench and the line. Every repaired feeder is mounted on a reference, struck through several feed steps, compared with a known centre, adjusted if needed, rechecked, and only then signed off. The gate adds minutes per feeder and removes the uncertainty from the most uncertain feeders you own.

On the FUJI NXT Feeder Calibration Jig the gate takes a few steps: mount the feeder with the calibration ruler, press Auto/Manual, watch the cross cursor at 50X, adjust the feeder bolt-pin until the component centre and the cursor coincide, check the wheel gear and lock the screws. The X, Y and H wheels were set and locked once against the ruler, so every repaired feeder is judged against the same point.

Keep the recheck results next to the repair record. When the same feeder fails its recheck twice, the record makes the decision for you: the problem is wear, not adjustment, and the feeder needs parts or retirement. That is how the repair bench gets better each month instead of busier.

Two senior technicians look at the same feeder. One says it is fine. The other says it is out. Both have fifteen years of experience, and the line is waiting for one of them to be right.

The argument is not about skill. It is about the reference. When the only reference is a technician's eye and memory, each person carries a slightly different idea of correct, and each shift calibrates to its own idea. The result is feeders that pass on days and fail on nights - and a team that trusts each other a little less every time it happens.

Replace opinion with one physical reference that everyone checks against. Define it once, lock it, protect it, and make every judgement a comparison with it. When the comparison is visible on a screen, the conversation changes from who is right to what the screen shows.

Wear does not arrive on the day the throw rate jumps. It arrives months earlier, a few microns at a time, on a lever and a tape-guide cover nobody looks at closely.

A worn lever, a tired thimble or a scuffed tape-guide cover changes how the tape is advanced and held. The feeder still feeds, so it passes the quick check on the line. Then the margin runs out, the throw rate climbs on a handful of slots, and the team starts replacing feeders in a hurry - often the wrong ones.

Look for wear on purpose, on a schedule, at a magnification that shows it. Strike the lever slowly and watch the movement, then at speed. Look at the thimble rising and falling, the lever contact surfaces and the tape-guide cover. Note what you see per feeder, and compare with the last check instead of with memory.

One good technician can keep forty feeders accurate. Four hundred feeders across three shifts need something that does not live in one person's head.

Most feeder rooms grow by adding people, not by adding a standard. Each new technician learns from the last one, the method drifts, records live in notebooks, and the knowledge leaves when the person leaves. The room gets bigger without getting more reliable.

Scale a feeder room with three fixed things: one reference, one procedure and one record. The reference is physical and locked. The procedure is short enough to fit on a card. The record captures feeder ID, date, observation, adjustment and recheck. Add stations by copying these three things, not by hiring another expert.

If your feeders only get attention when the line stops, your maintenance schedule is being written by your worst feeder.

Crisis maintenance feels efficient because nothing is checked that is not broken. In practice it means every feeder issue is found at the most expensive moment - during production - and every fix is rushed. The same feeders fail again because nobody had time to find out why.

Split your feeders into rotation groups and check one group each week, whether it has given trouble or not. Combine that with event triggers: every repaired feeder, every incoming used feeder and every feeder pulled for a pick-up error goes to the bench. Calendar checks catch slow drift; event checks catch sudden faults.
